blocks.text: A fire crew must decide at what angle to aim a hose so the jet clears a wall and reaches a window 6 m up. The water leaves the nozzle as a stream of particles, each moving under gravity alone. Treating the horizontal and vertical motions separately turns this curved-path problem into two simple straight-line problems.

blocks.markdown: In **Cartesian curvilinear motion** the position of a particle in a plane is the vector $\mathbf r=x\,\mathbf i+y\,\mathbf j$ (m). Differentiating each component separately gives velocity $\mathbf v=\dot x\,\mathbf i+\dot y\,\mathbf j$ and acceleration $\mathbf a=\ddot x\,\mathbf i+\ddot y\,\mathbf j$. The unit vectors $\mathbf i,\mathbf j$ are fixed in direction, so no extra terms appear. The speed is $v=\sqrt{v_x^2+v_y^2}$ and the velocity is always tangent to the path.

blocks.title: Projectile (drag-free)
blocks.text: A projectile is a particle moving under gravity alone, with air resistance neglected. Its acceleration is $a_x=0$ and $a_y=-g$, with $g=9.81$ m/s$^2$, taking $y$ upward.

blocks.caption: Launch speed $v_0$ at angle $\theta$ above the horizontal.

blocks.markdown: The key idea is **independence of components**: the horizontal motion is uniform (constant $v_x$) and the vertical motion is constant acceleration $-g$. They share only the clock $t$. For launch and landing at the same height, the flight time is $T=2v_0\sin\theta/g$, the range is $R=v_x T$, and the highest point occurs when $v_y=0$.

blocks.caption: Valid for launch and landing at the same level, no drag.

blocks.title: Range and maximum height
blocks.prompt: A ball is launched from level ground at $v_0=25$ m/s at $\theta=40^\circ$. Find the flight time, range and maximum height ($g=9.81$ m/s$^2$).

steps.text: Time of flight: vertical velocity reverses.
Range from the uniform horizontal motion.

blocks.caption: The two components of projectile motion.

blocks.markdown: To find when a projectile reaches a **target at a given height** $y_T$, set $y(t)=y_T$. This is a quadratic in $t$ and gives up to two times: one on the way up and one on the way down. If the discriminant is negative, the target is never reached at that speed and angle. The horizontal position at the chosen time then follows from $x=v_0\cos\theta\,t$.

blocks.title: Time to reach a window
blocks.prompt: A hose jet leaves ground level at 18 m/s at $55^\circ$ above the horizontal. At what times is it 6 m above the ground? ($g=9.81$ m/s$^2$.)
blocks.answer: The jet is 6 m high at $t\approx0.49$ s on the way up and again at $t\approx2.52$ s on the way down.

items: Choose axes and the positive direction first; $g$ is negative if $y$ is up.
Resolve the launch velocity into $v_0\cos\theta$ and $v_0\sin\theta$.
Use the vertical equations to find times, the horizontal equation for distances.
Check roots physically: reject negative times and note two solutions for a target below the apex.

blocks.title: Common errors
blocks.text: Never include $g$ in the horizontal equation, and never use the range formula when launch and landing heights differ; for a general target use $y(t)$ and solve the quadratic. The speed at the apex is $v_0\cos\theta$, not zero.

points: Resolve position, velocity and acceleration into fixed Cartesian components and treat each direction separately.
A drag-free projectile has $a_x=0$, $a_y=-g$, giving $T=2v_0\sin\theta/g$, $R=v_0^2\sin2\theta/g$, $H=v_0^2\sin^2\theta/(2g)$ for equal launch and landing heights.
A target at height $y_T$ is reached at the roots of $y(t)=y_T$, which may be two, one or none.

questions.stem: Neglecting air resistance, what is the horizontal component of acceleration of a projectile during flight?

distractorRationale.a: This is the vertical acceleration, not the horizontal one.
distractorRationale.b: This would arise only for motion on an incline, not free flight.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: only gravity acts, and it is vertical, so $a_x=0$.

questions.explanation: With drag neglected the only force is the weight, which is vertical. Hence $a_x=0$ and the horizontal velocity stays constant throughout the flight.

questions.stem: A drag-free projectile is at the highest point of its path. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Its velocity and acceleration are both zero
Its velocity is zero but its acceleration is $g$ downward
Its velocity is horizontal and its speed is $v_0\cos\theta$

questions.correctOptionText: Its velocity is horizontal and its speed is $v_0\cos\theta$

distractorRationale.a: Acceleration is still $g$ downward at every instant.
distractorRationale.b: Only the vertical component of velocity is zero, not the whole velocity.
distractorRationale.c: The speed is $v_0$ only at launch (and landing at the same level).

questions.explanation: At the apex the vertical velocity component vanishes, but the horizontal component is unchanged at $v_0\cos\theta$. Gravity acts throughout, so the acceleration is never zero.

questions.stem: Two identical shots leave level ground at the same speed, one at $30^\circ$ and one at $60^\circ$ above the horizontal, with no drag. Compare them.

options.text: Equal ranges; the $60^\circ$ shot reaches a greater height and flies longer
Equal ranges and equal flight times
The $30^\circ$ shot has the greater range
The $60^\circ$ shot has the greater range and the same height

questions.correctOptionText: Equal ranges; the $60^\circ$ shot reaches a greater height and flies longer

distractorRationale.a: Correct: $\sin 60^\circ=\sin(2\times 30^\circ)$ identical range; the vertical component and so $H$ and $T$ are larger at $60^\circ$.
distractorRationale.b: Flight time depends on $v_0\sin\theta$, which differs.
distractorRationale.c: Range depends on $\sin2\theta$, and $\sin60^\circ=\sin120^\circ$ so they are equal.

questions.explanation: The range $R=v_0^2\sin2\theta/g$ is the same for complementary angles because $\sin(2\theta)=\sin(180^\circ-2\theta)$. The steeper shot has a larger vertical velocity so it climbs higher and stays aloft longer.

questions.stem: A particle moves with $x=2t^3$ and $y=5t^2$ (metres, $t$ in s). Its acceleration magnitude at $t=2$ s is

distractorRationale.a: This is the speed $\sqrt{24^2+20^2}$, not the acceleration.
distractorRationale.d: Adds the components arithmetically ($24+10$) instead of vectorially.

questions.explanation: Differentiate twice: $\ddot x=12t$ and $\ddot y=10$. At $t=2$ s, $a_x=24$ m/s$^2$ and $a_y=10$ m/s$^2$, so $a=\sqrt{576+100}=26.0$ m/s$^2$.

questions.stem: A football is kicked from level ground at 22 m/s at $35^\circ$ above the horizontal. Neglecting drag and taking $g=9.81$ m/s$^2$, find its maximum height in metres.
questions.explanation: The vertical launch component is $22\sin35^\circ=12.62$ m/s. The apex is where $v_y=0$, so $H=v_y^2/(2g)=159.2/19.62=8.12$ m.

questions.stem: A stone is thrown horizontally at 15 m/s from the edge of a 45 m cliff. Taking $g=9.81$ m/s$^2$ and no drag, find the time to reach the sea level at the foot of the cliff, in seconds.
questions.explanation: The initial vertical velocity is zero, so $45=\tfrac12(9.81)t^2$ and $t=\sqrt{90/9.81}=3.03$ s. The horizontal speed does not affect the fall time.

questions.stem: A drone's velocity has components $v_x=12$ m/s and $v_y=-5$ m/s in a fixed Cartesian frame. Find its speed in m/s.
questions.explanation: Speed is the magnitude of the velocity vector, $\sqrt{12^2+(-5)^2}=\sqrt{169}=13$ m/s. The negative sign shows downward motion but does not change the magnitude.

questions.stem: A ball is thrown from a height of 1.2 m above level ground at 18 m/s at $50^\circ$ above the horizontal. Taking $g=9.81$ m/s$^2$ and no drag, find the time until it strikes the ground, in seconds.
Explain why setting $y(t)=y_T$ for a projectile can give two valid times, one valid time or none, and explain how you would decide which to use for a target on a rising path.
markingGuide: $y(t)$ is quadratic in $t$ so the equation has up to two roots.
Two positive roots: the particle passes the height on the way up and again on the way down.
One root (double) when the target height equals the apex.
No real root (negative discriminant) when the target is above the apex, so it is unreachable.
Negative or unphysical roots are rejected; choose the first positive root for the rising pass or the later one for the descending pass as the problem states.
questions.explanation: The vertical position is parabolic in time, so a horizontal line at the target height can cut it in two points, touch it, or miss it. The discriminant tells you which case applies.

questions.stem: Starting from the component equations, derive the range $R=v_0^2\sin2\theta/g$ for level ground, state the assumptions, and use it to explain why complementary angles give equal ranges.
markingGuide: Assume drag neglected, constant $g$, and launch and landing at the same height.
Substitute into $x=v_0\cos\theta\,T$ and use $2\sin\theta\cos\theta=\sin2\theta$ to obtain $R$.
Complementary angles $\theta$ and $90^\circ-\theta$ give $\sin2\theta$ equal, hence equal $R$.
questions.explanation: The range follows from multiplying the uniform horizontal speed by the flight time. Since $\sin(180^\circ-2\theta)=\sin2\theta$, angles that sum to $90^\circ$ share the same range.
